procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated January 8, 1969 of the Bombay High Court in Criminal Application No. 1341 of 1968 refusing to quash the order of committal passed by the Magistrate.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant filed an application in the High Court under sec. 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure to quash the committal order. The appellant argued that no consent, as required by s. 196A(1) Cr.P.C., having been obtained, the Magistrate had no jurisdiction to take cognizance of the offence of conspiracy. The High Court dismissed the application.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave against the High Court's judgment. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Magistrate lacked jurisdiction to take cognizance of the case because prior consent under Section 196A(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code, required for an offence of criminal conspiracy, was not obtained.

facts: The police filed a charge-sheet against the appellant for offences including abetment of forgery and impersonation (ss. 419/109, 468, and 471, I.P.C.).
The police charge-sheet did not mention or allege the offence of criminal conspiracy under section 120B.

The Magistrate, after reviewing the charge-sheet and other documents, framed charges against the appellant that included criminal conspiracy (s. 120B) to commit the non-cognizable offence of forging a passport.
The appellant argued that since the Magistrate framed a charge for criminal conspiracy, prior consent under Section 196A(2) of the Cr.P.C. was required, and its absence invalidated the proceedings.
law: Section 196A(2) of the Cr.P.C. prohibits a court from taking cognizance of the offence of criminal conspiracy to commit a non-cognizable offence without prior government consent.
Taking cognizance is the initial step a Magistrate takes based on a complaint or police report (charge-sheet) under Section 190 of the Cr.P.C.

The test for whether sanction is required depends on the offence "primarily and essentially" disclosed by the facts in the initial complaint or charge-sheet, not necessarily the final charges framed by the court.
application: The Court distinguished between the initial act of "taking cognizance" and the later act of "framing charges."
It reasoned that the Magistrate took cognizance of the offences that were actually alleged in the police charge-sheet, which were abetment of forgery and impersonation.
The offence of criminal conspiracy was not alleged in the charge-sheet, so the Magistrate did not take cognizance of it at the initial stage.
The fact that the Magistrate later decided that the evidence warranted a charge of criminal conspiracy did not change the nature of the offence for which he had originally taken cognizance.
Applying the "primarily and essentially" test, the Court found that the charge-sheet and witness statements disclosed an offence of abetment, not criminal conspiracy.
Since the cognizance was taken for abetment, an offence for which no prior consent is needed, the requirement of Section 196A(2) was not triggered.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's contention, holding that the Magistrate had taken cognizance of the offence of abetment as presented in the police charge-sheet, not criminal conspiracy. Therefore, the requirement for prior consent under Section 196A(2) did not apply, and the Magistrate acted within his jurisdiction.

issue.issue_text: Whether the determination of an offence for the purpose of taking cognizance depends on the sections cited in the charge-sheet or on the offence prima facie disclosed by the facts and allegations.

facts: The police submitted a charge-sheet against the accused for offences including abetment of forgery and false impersonation.
The charge-sheet did not refer to or charge the accused with the offence of criminal conspiracy (s. 120B, I.P.C.).
The Magistrate took cognizance of the case based on this charge-sheet.
At a later stage, when framing charges for committal, the Magistrate concluded that a charge of criminal conspiracy was more appropriate based on the materials.
The issue arose whether the Magistrate's initial cognizance was invalid because the necessary prior consent for a conspiracy charge (under s. 196A(2) Cr.P.C.) had not been obtained.
law: When a Magistrate takes cognizance of an offence under s. 190, Cr.P.C. upon a police report, they do so based on the offence or offences disclosed in that report.

The determination of which offence is being considered for cognizance depends not on the specific sections of law cited in the complaint or charge-sheet, but on the offence that is 'prima facie' or 'primarily and essentially' disclosed by the facts and allegations within it.
The proper test is to examine the allegations in the complaint/charge-sheet to see what offence is primarily and essentially disclosed.
application: The Court applied the principle that the substance of the allegations, not the section numbers, is what matters for taking cognizance.

It observed that the charge-sheet submitted to the magistrate did not allege criminal conspiracy. Instead, the allegations 'primarily and essentially' disclosed offences of abetment of forgery and false impersonation.
Therefore, the Court concluded that the Magistrate initially took cognizance only of the offences alleged in the charge-sheet (abetment, forgery, etc.).
The Magistrate's later decision to frame a charge for criminal conspiracy was a separate step that occurred after cognizance had already been validly taken.
Because cognizance was taken for offences that did not require prior consent, the proceedings were validly initiated.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the determination of an offence for the purpose of taking cognizance depends on the offence prima facie disclosed by the facts and allegations in the police report or complaint, not merely on the sections of law cited. In this case, since the charge-sheet primarily disclosed offences of abetment and forgery, the magistrate took cognizance of those offences, and the subsequent framing of a conspiracy charge did not invalidate the initial cognizance.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Magistrate lacked jurisdiction to take cognizance of the case because prior consent under Section 196A(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code, required for an offence of criminal conspiracy, was not obtained.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that since the Magistrate ultimately framed a charge for criminal conspiracy (Section 120B) in the committal order, the entire proceeding was invalid from the start.

He contended that because taking cognizance of criminal conspiracy requires prior consent under Section 196A(2), and no such consent was obtained, the Magistrate acted without jurisdiction, and the committal order should be quashed.
respondent_arguments: The Magistrate took cognizance based on the police charge-sheet, which did not charge the accused with criminal conspiracy.
The offences alleged in the charge-sheet at the time of taking cognizance (e.g., cheating, forgery, abetment) did not require prior consent under Section 196A.
The decision to frame a charge for criminal conspiracy was made at a later stage (the committal order), after cognizance had already been validly taken.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the determination of an offence for the purpose of taking cognizance depends on the sections cited in the charge-sheet or on the offence prima facie disclosed by the facts and allegations.
appellant_arguments: The appellant's position implies that the offence for which charges are ultimately framed should determine the validity of the initial cognizance, meaning the substance of the allegations from the start pointed to a conspiracy that required sanction, regardless of the sections initially cited.
respondent_arguments: The question of whether sanction is necessary depends not on the sections mentioned in a complaint or charge-sheet, but on the offence 'prima facie' disclosed by the facts and allegations contained within it.
The proper test is to examine the complaint to see what offence is 'primarily and essentially' disclosed at the time of taking cognizance.

cases.principle: The proper test to determine if consent for prosecution is necessary is whether the allegations made in the complaint disclosed 'primarily and essentially' an offence for which such consent would be necessary, rather than just looking at the offences mentioned in the heading or the use of specific expressions.
It is not the sections of law referred to which matter, but the offence that is prima facie disclosed by the facts.
The question of whether sanction is necessary depends not on the sections referred to in a complaint but on the offence prima facie disclosed by the facts alleged in it.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The determination of whether sanction is necessary to initiate proceedings depends not on the sections of law cited in a complaint or charge-sheet, but on the offence that is primarily and essentially disclosed by the facts and allegations contained therein.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The validity of a Magistrate's action in taking cognizance of a case is determined by the offences alleged in the charge-sheet at that specific moment, not by the charges that may be framed at a later stage. Since the charge-sheet did not allege criminal conspiracy, the Magistrate validly took cognizance of the offences mentioned therein. The subsequent framing of a conspiracy charge in the committal order did not retroactively invalidate the initial cognizance for lack of prior consent under Section 196A(2) of the Cr.P.C., as that consent was not a condition precedent at the time cognizance was taken.
legal_tests_applied: The proper test should be whether the allegations made in the petition of complaint disclosed primarily and essentially an offence or offences for which a consent in writing would be necessary to the initiation of the proceedings within the meaning of s. 196A(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
The question whether sanction is necessary or not depends not on the sections referred to in a complaint but the offence prima facie disclosed by the facts alleged in it.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's argument failed because the court distinguished between the stage of taking cognizance and the later stage of framing charges. The court found that at the time of taking cognizance, the charge-sheet did not refer to or charge the accused with criminal conspiracy.

The Magistrate's decision to frame a charge for criminal conspiracy was made only at the later stage of passing the committal order, after cognizance had already been validly taken based on the initial allegations.

Consequently, the court concluded: "Therefore, the Magistrate did not take cognizance of the offence under s. 120B, I.P.C., and hence, consent under s. 196A(2) Cr.P.C., was not a condition precedent."
why_respondent_won: The respondent's position was accepted because the court agreed that the Magistrate's jurisdiction is fixed at the moment of taking cognizance. The court stated, "The cognizance which the Magistrate took was therefore, only of the offences alleged in the charge-sheet..."
The court adopted the legal test that the necessity of sanction depends on the offence 'prima facie' and 'primarily and essentially' disclosed by the facts, not the specific sections mentioned.

Applying this test, the court found that the offence 'primarily and essentially' disclosed in the charge-sheet was one of abetment of forgery and false impersonation, for which no prior consent was required.
